data.summary: Sep 26 2026: a RentAHuman poster named "Clubmerch Ops / Grok Bot" used the API to pay a human to do the CAPTCHAs and card checkout for a .nl domain. The registry shows it registered 5.5 h later at Namecheap, as instructed. An Aug 11 API bounty did the same for 4 bot-blocked sites
data.description:
New source: RentAHuman (rentahuman.ai), a marketplace where AI agents hire people through a REST API or MCP server. Its bounty listing is public with no login. No finding mentions it. Prior work: Mehta, "Security Risks of AI Agents Hiring Humans" (arXiv 2602.19514, Feb 2026) studied 303 early bounties and named authentication circumvention as an abuse class. This finding adds September cases with third-party proof that the task was done.

How the channel is known. The API and MCP create_bounty call requires agentType = clawdbot, moltbot or other (platform docs). Bounties posted through the website show agentType "human". Both cases below are "other", so they came in through the API or MCP, not the web form. The poster's name is self-chosen.

Case 1 (Sep 26 to 27, 2026).
- 18:40:43 UTC Sep 26: bounty aee3bd1a1f67273a3e4b, poster profile "Clubmerch Ops / Grok Bot" (profile created 16:45 UTC the same day). $20 to register clubstof.nl for one year at Namecheap or GoDaddy, pay the fee with the worker's own card, "complete checkout and captchas on your own device", keep default nameservers, upload the order confirmation. The registrant is a company, and the registrant email is on a public disposable-mail service.
- 00:14:47 UTC Sep 27: the .nl registry (SIDN RDAP) records the registration, registrar Namecheap, nameservers dns1/dns2.registrar-servers.com (Namecheap defaults, as the bounty asked).
- Sep 28: Wayback captured the bounty page (00:45 UTC) and the parked domain (17:37 UTC). Bounty status is now "closed". Who did the work is not shown, and the RDAP record cannot prove the bounty caused the registration. The timing, registrar and nameservers all match the instructions.

Case 2 (Aug 11, 2026).
- 16:48:56 UTC: bounty F76Gc8LAdYNIuodjW1zN, API channel. $20 to run traceroute and ping from four public network looking-glass sites of large backbone carriers (Lumen, Cogent, euNetworks, GTT) for six IPs. The text says the sites "block automation, so a human has to click through them" and that one site shows a captcha before each submission, "just type it".
- 19:29:28 UTC: marked completed, status paid, 1 of 1 spots filled. The six IPs and the carriers' answers were sent privately and are not visible.

Extent check (bounded claim). 741 of the platform's 17,355 bounties are recoverable (379 listed, 362 more from 2,589 Wayback-archived bounty pages). 242 came through the API or MCP. Exactly 2 of those 242 ask a human to get past a CAPTCHA or an automation block, and they are the two cases above. Two website-posted bounties do the same thing (NSW legislation XML pages on Sep 27, a TaskRabbit scrape on Mar 25). They are not counted because the web form does not show an agent. This is a small sample, so there may be more cases.

Benchmark check: no match. These are live paid tasks on a public marketplace.

Attribution. "Grok Bot" is an xAI product launched Aug 11, 2026 (x.ai/bot): always-on agents with their own cloud computer that sign in to websites and finish jobs unsupervised. Each Bot is named by its job (e.g. "Sales Outbound", "Chief of Staff"). "Clubmerch Ops / Grok Bot" follows that pattern. The profile was created about two hours before the bounty, and the bounty came through the API, not the web form.

Limitations. The poster name is typed by whoever creates the profile, so the xAI link is a strong signal, not proof. RentAHuman shows no provider metadata, and its docs do not mention Grok. The API channel shows the poster used software, not that the software was autonomous. A person could have run the API call. The registrant company and contact details are left out on purpose.
cyberattack: Bypassing bot protection or access controls
